program: Free primary, specialty, dental, mental health and pharmacy care

what: CommunityHealth provides volunteer-supported primary, specialty, medication and mental-health care for Chicago adults.
Current eligibility generally requires no insurance or HBIS only, with household income at or below 300% of federal poverty guidelines.
The annual illustration includes short health relief and signed household financial protection, not retail donated care or a priced marginal gift.
strengths: Unique annual patients prevent adding visits and prescriptions as extra people.
Original audited expenses include recognized donated resources.
Free-care access offers a plausible financial-protection mechanism.
reservations: Clinical utility and net cash effects are hypotheses, not measured recipient effects.
Donated drug accounting is not economic opportunity cost.
Clinical capacity, patient residence and gift-created expansion remain unmeasured.

sections.what: CommunityHealth provides medical, dental, medication and mental health care at Chicago sites. Its giving page identifies EIN 36-3831793. Dental waiting lists indicate unmet demand but do not establish whether money or volunteers constrain supply. Current eligibility includes HBIS-only patients, and services now explicitly accept no new dental referrals. Documentation and interpreting requirements may create access costs; no clinical outcomes are inferred from registration.
sections.monitoring: The 2024 report counts 4,147 patients, 24,695 visits and 23,579 prescriptions. Only patients enter the model, preventing duplicate credit across services. Request baseline illness, deduplicated clinical response, sustained utility, alternative care and resident county. The Oregon randomized Medicaid study increased utilization and reduced depression but found no significant measured physical-health gains in two years; coverage is not a direct trial of this clinic, and supplies no numerical calibration here. Root freshly recovered the original annual page: 1,888 new registrations are not added to 4,147 annual patients. Original Oregon Medicaid financial results show reduced out-of-pocket spending, but insurance is not this clinic and its physical-health null does not calibrate these patients' utility.
sections.qualitative: Primary and medication access can provide pain, mental-health and financial-strain relief. The original Oregon trial's $215.35 annual out-of-pocket difference is not a CommunityHealth effect or a disposable earnings estimate. A $200 otherwise-paid medical cash hypothesis and .3 financial-protection additionality are explicit transport judgments after alternative providers and benefit changes. Earnings are zero centrally as an uncertainty judgment, with positive and negative tests; unpaid time savings are not wages. Other health, education and resource channels remain unmeasured, not proven zero.
sections.cost: Root freshly verified original 2024 full expense $21,453,697, including $12,728,899 consumed inventory, $3,995,847 donated services and $177,307 other in-kind expense. Those resources are not added again. Removing the separate .4 marginal gift multiplier makes the annual-work boundary coherent, not more empirically effective. Clinical patient count remains 4,147, while .8 grouping affects only household resources. Full .05 aggregate process harm is judged and independent of success. Whole annual cost against bounded selected effects is not calibrated portfolio expected value. Current health30.43145 and signed resources+.40210 give about $6.96M per ten combined equivalents.
sections.funding: Fresh original audit revenue $21,052,293, net assets $6,621,698, donor restrictions $684,948 and government grants $1,000,893 remain relevant to gift uncertainty. Cash-like $4,551,644 expense excludes $16,902,053 recognized in-kind, not cash flow or full economic opportunity cost. Resource households with judged financial protection jointly receive positive net cash and any net work gain, reduced only for positive overlap, minus full $25 incremental travel/time/access burden relative to alternative care; other exposed households retain the full burden. Baseline $20,000 is judged consumption, not eligibility income or measured earnings. Distinct external provider/payer stresses retain full losses for local recipients, excluding recognized resources already in the numerator; zero central external loss is a donor-budget boundary convention, not proof of no incidence. Free public and charity care, HBIS and deferred treatment are alternatives. Actual other cash effects, earnings, volunteer opportunity costs beyond recognition and priced gift capacity remain unknown.

sources.title: Original Oregon Medicaid randomized clinical and financial outcomes
sources.publisher: New England Journal of Medicine / MIT author-hosted manuscript

model.formula: Health=g*(N*a*u*T-full aggregate process harm)/(1+r)^delay. Resources=.5*sum(people*discounted finite years*log(after/before)*geography), household joint changes and positive-only overlap; price10=10*C/(health+signed resources).
model.costScope: Full audited recipient costs including recognized donated resources; external hospital resources not included. Recognized pharmaceutical wholesale values and donated-provider billing rates are accounting amounts, not measured opportunity costs.
model.counterfactual: Alternative clinic/public/HBIS care and ineffective treatment via clinical a; financial protection has independent resourceAdditional hypothesis, not clinical response gating. Annual cost receives no marginal financing multiplier.
model.geographicAttribution: Current service sites are in Cook County. g=.98 is judged resident share, not observed; pinned 13-county MSA excludes Kenosha.
model.uncertainty: Central illustrative scenario and favorable/poor bounds are judgments, not calibrated EV or confidence interval. Cross-recipient results cannot be summed without deduplication. These costs are whole-portfolio equivalents, not marginal gift purchase guarantees. Cost numerators use different accounting recognition of donated care; central prices must not be interpreted as a comparable economic-efficiency ranking. Favorable and poor scenarios are illustrative cases, not exhaustive bounds.
